chapters.title: Chapter 2: Listed Shares and Equity Mutual Funds

lessons.title: Equity Mutual Funds, ETFs and SIPs: FIFO and Unit-Wise Holding Periods

body.text: A SIP is not one investment. It is a string of separate purchases, each with its own date, its own cost and its own tax clock. Redeem without knowing which units go first and you can end up paying 20% on money you thought was long-term.

children.text: Pooja, a 30-year-old doctor in Noida, started a ₹10,000 monthly SIP in a Nifty 50 index fund in January 2025. In September 2026 she redeemed ₹2 lakh for her sister's wedding. Her SIP was "over 18 months old", so she expected only long-term gains, comfortably within the ₹1.25 lakh exemption. Her capital gains statement showed a short-term gain too. Here is why.
Step 1: Is the Fund Equity-Oriented?

markDefs.definition: A mutual fund scheme that invests more than 65% of its total proceeds in equity shares of domestic listed companies, or a fund of funds that invests at least 90% in listed ETFs which themselves invest at least 90% in such shares.

children.text: The 20% and 12.5% equity rates from the last lesson apply only to an
equity-oriented fund

. That means more than 65% of the portfolio in shares of Indian listed companies, or a fund of funds putting at least 90% into ETFs that themselves hold at least 90% in such shares. The name on the fund means nothing on its own. The portfolio decides.

body.title: Which Fund Gets Equity Treatment?
body.question: You have held each of these for 15 months. Which one qualifies for the 12.5% rate with the ₹1.25 lakh exemption?
options: A Nasdaq 100 fund of funds bought on Groww
A gold ETF bought on NSE through Zerodha
A flexi cap fund that keeps about 70% in Indian listed shares and the rest in US stocks and cash
body.explanation: The flexi cap fund has more than 65% in Indian listed equity, so it is equity-oriented. The Nasdaq 100 fund of funds is 15 months old but on the 24-month clock, so its gain is still short-term. The gold ETF is long-term after 12 months but taxed at 12.5% under section 197 with no exemption. The liquid fund is always short-term.

children.text: Step 2: Every Instalment Is Its Own Lot

Each SIP instalment buys units at that day's NAV. Those units carry that date as their purchase date and that NAV as their cost. Your January 2025 units and your August 2026 units sit in the same folio, but for tax they are completely different assets.

markDefs.definition: The rule that the units or shares acquired first are treated as the ones sold or redeemed first. Fund houses apply it within each folio, and it applies within each demat account for units and shares held in demat form.

children.text: When you redeem, units go out on a
first in, first out (FIFO)

basis. Your oldest units are redeemed first, then the next oldest, and so on. You cannot pick which lot to redeem. Fund houses apply FIFO folio by folio, and brokers apply it demat account by demat account.

body.title: Pooja's Monthly SIP: Units Bought Each Month (₹10,000 per instalment)

body.text: Look at the chart. When NAV dips, the same ₹10,000 buys more units, which is the whole point of a SIP. But every bar is a separate lot with its own purchase price and its own 12-month clock.

body.title: Count the Long-Term Lots
body.prompt: Pooja's SIP instalments went in on the 1st of every month from 1 January 2025 to 1 September 2026, 21 instalments in total. She redeems on 20 September 2026. How many of her 21 instalments have been held for more than 12 months?
body.explanation: Instalments from 1 January 2025 to 1 September 2025 have all been held for more than 12 months by 20 September 2026. That is 9 lots. The 1 October 2025 instalment is still short of 12 months, as are all 12 instalments after it.

body.caption: Pooja redeems ₹2,00,000 at a NAV of ₹188 on 20 September 2026 (NAVs illustrative; stamp duty and exit load ignored)

cells: Long-term: all 9 lots from Jan to Sep 2025
Short-term: part of the lots from Oct 2025 onwards
Total

children.text: FIFO used up all 9 long-term lots first, but those only covered 577.284 units. The rest of her ₹2 lakh came from newer, short-term units. Her ₹18,529 long-term gain is fully covered by the ₹1.25 lakh exemption, but the ₹7,361 short-term gain is taxed at 20%: ₹1,472 before cess.

body.title: Could Pooja Have Avoided the Short-Term Gain?
body.scenario: On 20 September 2026, Pooja's 9 long-term lots hold 577.284 units in total, bought for ₹90,000. At a NAV of ₹188, they are worth ₹1,08,529. She needs ₹2,00,000, but the wedding is still six weeks away.
body.prompt: Suggest two ways she could reduce or avoid the short-term capital gains tax.
body.modelAnswer: First, she could redeem only ₹1,08,529 now. Because of FIFO, that exactly uses up her long-term units, giving a long-term gain of ₹18,529, well within the ₹1.25 lakh exemption and so tax-free. Second, she could spread redemptions over the next six weeks. Each month another SIP lot crosses the 12-month mark (the 1 October 2025 lot becomes long-term on 2 October 2026, and so on), so later redemptions carry fewer short-term units. She should also check whether any exit load applies and whether pausing new SIP instalments into the same folio suits her plans, since fresh units always join the back of the FIFO queue.

children.text: ELSS: Two Separate Clocks

body.label: ELSS Lock-In
body.context: Each ELSS SIP instalment is locked in for three years from its own date. A SIP started in April 2024 does not become fully free in April 2027; the March 2025 instalment stays locked until March 2028. Since every unlocked unit is well over 12 months old, ELSS redemptions are always long-term for tax.

children.text: Which Actions Count as a Redemption?

columns.label: Treated as a Transfer (Gain Taxed)
points: Redeeming units, whether lump sum or partial
Each SWP withdrawal, which redeems units on FIFO
Each STP instalment out of a fund into another fund
Switching between schemes, or between regular and direct plans
Selling ETF units on NSE or BSE

columns.label: Not a Transfer (No Gain Yet)
points: SEBI-driven merger or consolidation of two schemes; your original cost and date carry over
Converting units from statement form to demat form
Units passing to a nominee or legal heir on death
IDCW reinvestment, which is taxed as dividend income and creates new units with a new date
Changing the bank account or broker platform you view the holding on

body.title: SWP and Tax
body.textWithBlank: Under a systematic withdrawal plan, only the capital gain on the units redeemed is taxed, not the full withdrawal, because each withdrawal is a ___ of units.
body.explanation: Each SWP instalment redeems units, oldest first. Part of each withdrawal is simply your own cost coming back, and only the gain on those units is taxed. That is why SWPs from equity funds held for a long time can be very tax-efficient.

body.text: IDCW (dividend) payouts and reinvestments are not capital gains. They are dividend income, added to your total income and taxed at your slab rate. For most growing investors, the growth option is more tax-efficient because gains are taxed only when you redeem, at equity capital gains rates.

children.text: ETFs: Mutual Fund Units That Trade Like Shares
Bought and sold on the exchange:
the trade date on your contract note starts and ends the holding period, just like shares.
FIFO applies per demat account:
Nifty BeES units held with Zerodha and Groww are separate queues.
STT on the sale:
equity ETF sales on the exchange attract STT, which keeps them within sections 196 and 198.
Non-equity ETFs are different:
gold, silver and international ETFs become long-term after 12 months but are taxed under section 197 at 12.5% with no ₹1.25 lakh exemption, and short-term gains are taxed at your slab rate.

body.label: Get a Consolidated Capital Gains Statement on MF Central
body.description: MF Central, run jointly by CAMS and KFintech, lets you download a capital gains statement across all fund houses, with FIFO already applied lot by lot and gains split into short-term and long-term.

cards.definition: More than 65% in Indian listed equity, or a qualifying 90/90 fund of funds. Gets the equity rates.
Units bought on one date at one NAV. Every SIP instalment creates a new lot.
First in, first out. The oldest units in a folio or demat account are redeemed first.
Your account number with a fund house. FIFO runs separately in each folio.
Systematic withdrawal plan. Each withdrawal redeems units and only the gain on those units is taxed.
Income distribution cum capital withdrawal. Payouts are dividend income taxed at slab rate, not capital gains.

body.title: Before You Redeem a SIP Fund
steps: Confirm the fund is equity-oriented by checking the scheme information document or factsheet
Download a capital gains statement from MF Central or your fund house to see the lot-wise purchase dates
Work out how many units are long-term today and what they are worth
Redeem only that value if you want to avoid short-term gains, or spread redemptions over coming months
Check whether any exit load applies to the newest units
Keep your total long-term equity gains for the year in mind against the ₹1.25 lakh exemption

points: Equity rates apply only to funds with more than 65% in Indian listed equity, whatever the fund is called
Every SIP instalment is a separate lot with its own purchase date, cost and holding period
Redemptions follow FIFO, so the oldest units always go first, folio by folio or demat account by demat account
A partial redemption can mix long-term and short-term gains even in an old SIP
Switches, STPs and SWP withdrawals are all redemptions, while SEBI-driven scheme mergers are not
Gold, silver and international ETFs are listed but not equity, so they get no ₹1.25 lakh exemption

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and is not tax or investment advice. Fund examples describe categories, not recommendations, and NAVs used are illustrative. Sections and rates reflect the Income-tax Act, 2025 for tax year 2026-27. Verify a specific fund's tax classification in its scheme documents and consult a qualified tax professional before acting.
